summary: Salmon-Challis National Forest lookout staffed since at least 1920, rebuilt four times, with the current R-6 cab built in 1977 and still staffed each summer.

access.note: Drive-up access; generally staffed during fire season.

visit.trail_note: Lookout sits about half a mile south of the actual summit.

facts.agency: US Forest Service - Salmon-Challis National Forest

events.note: Telephone line construction crew strung a new line to Long Tom and Blue Nose mountains.
A lookout station already existed on Long Tom mountain; smoke chaser Frank L. Hall was injured near it.
Two-story log-framed cab built, the first of four structures on the mountain.
Replaced by a cabin and a barn.
L-4 cab on a log crib built in the 1940s.
High-frequency radio installed at Long Tom.
Chester "Chip" Beaty and Jeanne Kellar Beaty staffed the lookout 1949-1950; Jeanne's account was later published as "The Lookout Wife" in 1953.
Mr. and Mrs. Harold L. Edwards staffed the lookout.
Mr. and Mrs. Ralph Roads staffed the lookout; family drove up for a birthday dinner.
Current 10-foot concrete base with R-6 flat cab built between June 1 and October 5 by Wes Dana Sr., Jim Sherman, and Chuck Rummler, while Chet Rackham staffed the mountain that season.
Alexia Cochrane staffed the lookout as relief, 2007-2009.
Added to the National Historic Lookout Register, September 30, 2020.

evidence.quote: Wires will soon be stretched from Baldy mountain to Taylor mountain and from the mouth of Big creek to Long Tom and Blue Nose mountains.

evidence.supports: 1920 lookout station and Frank Hall injury
evidence.quote: He was brought to the lookout station on Long Tom mountain, where Dr. C. F. Hanmer was called to give him surgical aid.

The current structure is the fourth on Long Tom Mountain. A 2 story log cabin was constructed in 1923, replaced in 1933 and again in the 40's with a R1/L-4 cabin on a log crib.
Today's lookout was built in 1977 and is generally staffed during the fire season.

evidence.supports: 1923 two-story cab, 1977 R-6 cab on concrete base
1923, 1933 cabin and barn, 1940s L-4 cab, 1977 replacement, staffed every summer
evidence.quote: Long Tom has had a long history of structures, beginning with a 2-story log-frame cab in 1923, followed by a cabin and a barn in 1933. In the 1940's, an L-4 cab atop a log crib was built. This was ultimately replaced in 1977 with the current 10' concrete base with R-6 flat cab, located 1/2 mile south of the summit. It is staffed every summer.
1949: The catwalk was reconstructed by Joe Denny. (The Recorder-Herald)
July 13, 1950: "High frequency radio has been installed at Long Tom." (Recorder Herald)
July 12, 1951: "Mr. and Mrs. Harold L. Edwards, Orem, Utah, are at Long Tom." (The Recorder-Herald)

evidence.supports: 1972 Roads family staffing and birthday visit
evidence.quote: Family members prepared a ham and chicken dinner and drove to Long Tom fire lookout, Sunday to share the meal with Mr. and Mrs. Ralph Roads, who 'man' the lookout.

The new lookout was constructed between June 1 and Oct. 5. It was built by Wes Dana, Sr., carpenter; Jim Sherman and Chuck Rummler, helpers, and Chet Rackham, who is stationed at Long Tom as the Forest Service lookout.

1949–1950 Chester "Chip" Beaty Jeanne Kellar Beaty
1953: "The Lookout Wife" was published about Jeanne's account of living at Long Tom Lookout.

evidence.supports: Alexia Cochrane staffed 1986 and as relief 2007-2009

notes_for_editor: Fact-check pass 2026-10-04: the original research under-cited idahofirelookouts.com's known-staff list, crediting Alexia Cochrane only as unspecified 'relief' staffing and omitting Chester "Chip" Beaty, Jeanne Kellar Beaty (1949-1950, and the 1953 book "The Lookout Wife" about Jeanne's time there), and Margie Cook (1974). The full list is now in events/evidence and the story names them. The 1920 Frank Hall newspaper accounts are strong evidence for an early lookout presence predating the first built structure by three years, worth flagging if the record's earliest date needs revision.
